title: When a ranking changes behaviour
bodyMd:
An online marketplace began displaying sellers in order of their recent sales. The company described the ranking as a neutral reflection of popularity. A researcher noted, however, that sellers near the top received far more views. Higher sales could raise a seller's position, but a higher position could also generate sales. The ranking was therefore both a record of past behaviour and an influence on future behaviour.

To investigate the second effect, the researcher proposed temporarily varying the order among sellers with similar recent sales and comparing subsequent purchases. The company objected that this would make the display less faithful to the ranking rule. That objection was correct but missed the purpose of the experiment: a small departure from the rule was precisely what could help distinguish the effect of visibility from the popularity that the rule purported to measure.
